page.title: When to use tinyactors
page.description: Why tinyactors fits an embedded event loop, what a crash keeps and how it compares with Temporal, Durable Objects, Rivet and XState.

hero.headline: Run statechart actors inside your own process
hero.lede: tinyactors embeds SCXML actors on your event loop across Node.js, Python, browsers and C. Your code owns the process, store, effects and cross-host placement while the core passes 191 W3C tests.

section.heading: tinyactors fits millions of in-process statechart actors
section.p: tinyactors fits when you need memory density, SCXML charts, event-based effects, simulated-clock tests and one core across runtimes.

item.text: Actors take about 530 bytes started and 120 hibernated; operations cost about the same at four million as at two. Idle actors hibernate and wake on events; two million actors ran with at most 1000 in memory.
Each actor runs an SCXML chart of states, events and transitions with JavaScript or Python expressions. SCXML invoke runs long operations per state, and QuickJS sandboxes user-uploaded charts.

A chart reaches the world only through sends to an I/O processor, a handler you give the host. Because effects are events, tests avoid mocking external services: test handlers record sends and answer, return errors or never reply.

item.term: Timeouts tested with a simulated clock
item.text: A SimulatedClock moves only when the test moves it: a timeout of an hour takes no time. A payment that retries every 30 seconds runs all three attempts in milliseconds, alongside property tests.
One C core runs the same tests and the same chart in Node.js, Python, C and browsers.

section.heading: Limits: SCXML charts, single hosts and changing APIs
section.p: tinyactors stops at SCXML charts inside single hosts under active development with frequent breaking changes.

item.text: Each actor runs an SCXML chart with JavaScript or Python expressions. Erlang and Akka actors run any code you give them.
Actors stay in their spawning host, so your program runs a named host per process. Placement, deployment, failover and transport between hosts are your program's work.
The README says tinyactors is under active development and makes frequent breaking changes. Follow each package release and upgrade change in the tinyactors changelog.

section.heading: A crash stops memory and keeps saved state
section.p: Actors live in process memory, so a crash stops every actor and keeps only what your program saved.

item.text: Host.restore runs a snapshot in this process or another with variables, queued events and pending timers. One snapshot holds two million actors in 165 MB.
Each hibernated blob carries its host's random identity, so a fresh host refuses blobs from another host. A host restored from the original host's snapshot accepts those blobs.
A restored host starts at snapshot time and accepts blobs hibernated since. Your program replays all other inputs after the snapshot from its own journal.
tinyactors saves blobs through your store and takes snapshots when asked, restoring with matching options. All storage I/O stays in your application layer.
Live migration updates actors at rest to a new chart while keeping sessions, states and queues. A send to a hibernated actor wakes it, while a send to an absent actor fails immediately.

section.heading: Portable charts and MIT license, build-bound snapshots
section.p: Charts, event boundaries and the MIT license move across runtimes, whereas snapshots require matching memory layout.

claim.statement: W3C SCXML charts meet code at events
claim.p: Each chart is a W3C SCXML document rather than a proprietary format.
Your code meets tinyactors only at event boundaries: inputs go in, and effects come out to your handlers.

claim.statement: Core passes all 191 W3C SCXML tests
claim.p: The C core passes all 191 automatic tests of the W3C SCXML conformance suite.
Every binding runs the same suite across Node.js, Python, C and browsers.
claim.source: Memory, capacity and performance, "Correct by the standard"

claim.statement: MIT license covers every tinyactors package
claim.p: Every package is MIT licensed, allowing you to use, change and ship tinyactors while keeping its copyright and permission notice.
Snapshots and blobs use tinyactors' own format, and a snapshot restores only on a build with the same memory layout.
Keep data that must last in your own database.
claim.source: Snapshots, "Restore with the options the snapshot had"

section.heading: tinyactors runs SCXML directly inside your own hosts
section.p: Temporal, Durable Objects and Rivet manage persistence or placement, whereas XState is inspired by SCXML.

claim.statement: Temporal runs a server; tinyactors runs in-process
claim.p: Self-hosted Temporal runs Temporal Server and persistence stores on Docker, Kubernetes or by hand.
Your program creates a tinyactors host object directly for tests and runtime, handling journaling and cross-host transport.
tinyactors compared with Temporal sets the two side by side: tests, crashes and running changes.

claim.statement: Durable Objects place Workers; tinyactors uses your process
claim.p: Cloudflare describes a Durable Object as a Worker that combines compute with storage, placed near its first request.
A tinyactors actor runs inside any server or browser tab your program operates, with storage under your control.

claim.statement: Rivet places durable processes; tinyactors pins to hosts
claim.p: Rivet describes its actors as durable processes in your backend, placed by Rivet Cloud or your control plane.
A tinyactors actor stays in the host that spawned it, and your program routes across hosts.

claim.statement: XState takes SCXML inspiration; tinyactors runs SCXML
claim.p: XState's README says it is inspired by the SCXML specification.
tinyactors runs SCXML documents themselves, the same chart in every language, and the C core passes 191 W3C tests.
claim.source: Memory, capacity and performance, "Correct by the standard"
